passages.t: Fire from heaven, and a feast
passages.happening:
‘When Solomon had finished praying, fire came down from heaven and consumed the burnt offering and the sacrifices, and the glory of the LORD filled the temple’ (verse 1). The priests cannot enter (verse 2). When the people see the fire and the glory, they bow with their faces to the ground and give thanks: “For He is good; His loving devotion endures forever” (verse 3).

The king and the people offer sacrifices, 22,000 oxen and 120,000 sheep, and dedicate the house (verses 4-5). The Levites play the instruments David made, and the priests sound the trumpets (verse 6). The feast lasts seven days, with a vast assembly ‘from Lebo-hamath to the Brook of Egypt’ (verse 8), and on the twenty-third day of the seventh month Solomon sends them home, ‘joyful and glad of heart for the good things that the LORD had done for David, for Solomon, and for His people Israel’ (verse 10).
passages.hearers:
Chapter 6 ended with Solomon's plea that God would hear prayer offered toward this house. Chapter 7 answers twice, first in fire and glory before all the people, then in words to Solomon alone.

The fire from heaven is the Chronicler's own addition to the Kings account. It recalls the fire that fell on Aaron's first sacrifices at the tabernacle and the fire that answered David at this same place, marking the altar as God's chosen place. Fire on a sacrifice was the clearest sign of acceptance an ancient worshiper could imagine; the same sign answered Elijah on Mount Carmel.

Most of the animals were peace offerings, whose meat the worshipers ate, so the dedication was a great national feast and not only a solemn rite. The courtyard itself was consecrated because the bronze altar could not hold everything. The festival fell in the seventh month, September to October: seven days for the altar, seven for the Feast of Booths, and a closing assembly. Lebo-hamath, probably in the northern Beqaa Valley of modern Lebanon, and the Brook of Egypt, usually identified with the Wadi el-Arish in northern Sinai, mark the widest ideal extent of Israel's land.
passages.later: At the first sacrifice in the tabernacle, ‘Fire came out from the presence of the LORD and consumed the burnt offering and the fat portions on the altar. And when all the people saw it, they shouted for joy and fell facedown’ (Leviticus 9:24).
passages.asks: The people went home glad of heart for the good things God had done. Ask when you last went home from worship glad. And ask which good things God has done that you have not yet given thanks for.

passages.happening:
The LORD appears to him at night and says, “I have heard your prayer and have chosen this place for Myself as a house of sacrifice” (verse 12). Then: “If I close the sky so there is no rain, or if I command the locust to devour the land, or if I send a plague among My people” (verse 13), “and if My people who are called by My name humble themselves and pray and seek My face and turn from their wicked ways, then I will hear from heaven, forgive their sin, and heal their land” (verse 14). ‘Now My eyes will be open and My ears attentive to the prayers offered in this place’ (verse 15).

To Solomon God promises an established throne if he walks as David walked (verses 17-18). But if they forsake God's commands and serve other gods, ‘then I will uproot Israel from the soil I have given them, and I will banish from My presence this temple I have sanctified for My Name’ (verse 20). When the temple is a heap of rubble, passersby will ask why, and the answer will be that they forsook the LORD (verses 21-22).
passages.hearers:
The private speech has a clear shape: God accepts the temple, gives a promise for the people, a promise and a condition for the king, and a warning for all. Verse 13 echoes the disasters Solomon had named in his prayer, drought, locusts and plague, which Israel's covenant had warned of long before. Verse 14 answers with four verbs for the people, humble, pray, seek and turn, and three for God, hear, forgive and heal. The order matters: the land is healed after the sin is forgiven. Verses 13 to 15 are found only in Chronicles; 1 Kings 9 tells the same appearance without them.

To humble oneself, kana, is a favorite word of the Chronicler, and the rest of the book tests this promise reign by reign. Rehoboam's leaders humble themselves and are spared. Manasseh, the worst of the kings, humbles himself in Babylon and is brought home. Zedekiah, the last king, does not humble himself, and the warning of verses 19 to 22 comes true when Babylon burns this house.

The warning uses a familiar ancient form: treaties often ended with curses on a vassal who broke faith. The picture of passersby asking why the land was ruined echoes Deuteronomy. The Chronicler's own readers stood on the far side of the warning, home from exile to a rebuilt temple and no king, and they could hear in verse 14 that the way back was still open.
passages.later: The phrase ‘called by My name’ (verse 14) returns in the New Testament when James quotes Amos at the council in Jerusalem: ‘and all the Gentiles who are called by My name, says the Lord who does these things’ (Acts 15:17). John wrote, ‘If we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness’ (1 John 1:9).
passages.hard:
Is 2 Chronicles 7:14 a promise to America, or to any modern nation?

The verse is one of the most quoted in the Old Testament, read at national prayer gatherings and printed on signs. People who love it should be heard first: most of them grieve over what they see, and the verse gives that grief somewhere to go besides anger. It puts prayer before outrage and confession before blame.

Readers disagree about how far it reaches. Many interpreters point out that in context the promise is addressed to Israel, the covenant people called by God's name, about a particular land and a particular temple, and that the healing in view is the lifting of drought, locusts and plague. No modern nation stands where Israel stood, and applying the verse to a country can confuse the church with a nation. Others argue that the principle is broader: God has always answered humble, repentant prayer, the New Testament calls the church God's people, and believers may rightly pray this way for the places where they live, trusting that God may bring real good through it. A middle view reads the verse as applying fully to the church as God's people, its promise kept in forgiveness and renewal, while leaving the outcome for any nation in God's hands.

The site's guide, Is 2 Chronicles 7:14 a Promise to America?, reads it this way. To Solomon's Israel the promise was concrete. Through Christ the people called by God's name now reach into every nation, and no nation owns them. The verse still promises that God hears his people's humble prayer and that his mercy has not run out. It does not promise any nation revival or political victory in exchange for prayer; even in Chronicles, humbling brought mercy, not greatness. Praying for one's country is right. The error begins when a nation takes the place of the people God calls his own.

On every reading the verse makes one demand, and it begins not with other people's sins but with God's people humbling themselves. The wicked ways to turn from are one's own.
passages.asks: Humble, pray, seek, turn: the four verbs begin with the people who pray them. Ask which of them is hardest for you. And ask what wicked ways you would need to turn from that are your own, not someone else's.
